subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Coffee: The Second Most Traded Commodity
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Coffee: The Second Most Traded Commodity.

hook.text: Coffee is the world's second most traded commodity after crude oil. Over 2 billion cups are drunk daily.

buildup.text: The global coffee industry is worth over $450 billion. It employs 125 million people from farm to cup.

discovery.text: Yet 80% of coffee farmers earn less than $2 per day. The value concentrates at the top of the supply chain.

twist.text: A $5 latte contains about 10 cents' worth of raw coffee beans. The farmer's share is shockingly small.

climax.text: This imbalance drives poverty, migration, and deforestation in the world's biggest coffee-growing nations.

punchline.text: Billions in profit, pennies for farmers. Coffee's economics are broken.

quiz.question: What percentage of a $5 latte goes to raw coffee beans?

details.summary: Coffee is often called the world's second most traded commodity after oil, though this is debated. What is undeniable is its enormous economic footprint: over 125 million people depend on coffee for their livelihoods, and the global market exceeds 450 billion dollars annually.
details.whyItMatters: Coffee's sheer economic scale means that price swings, climate shifts, and trade policies affect millions of vulnerable farming families worldwide.
takeaways: The global coffee market exceeds 450 billion dollars annually
Over 125 million people depend on coffee for income
Coffee is among the top traded agricultural commodities

faq.question: Is coffee really the second most traded commodity?
faq.answer: The claim is often repeated but hard to verify because commodity rankings depend on how trade is measured. By volume or value, oil, natural gas, and some metals rank higher. Coffee is consistently among the top traded agricultural commodities.

faq.question: How much coffee is produced worldwide each year?
faq.answer: Global production is roughly 170 million 60-kilogram bags per year, or about 10 billion kilograms. Brazil produces about a third of this total, followed by Vietnam, Colombia, and Ethiopia.
